# Introduction {#sec-intro}

When housing, food, and utility costs outpace wages, families look for an explanation.
Automation is one of the explanations most often reached for. Gallup finds that the share
of American workers who worry technology will make their job obsolete rose sharply between
2021 and 2023, with the increase concentrated among college educated workers
[@Gallup2023], and Pew reports that Americans expect automation to displace other people's
jobs more readily than their own [@Pew2017]. That worry is widespread, but it is a
perception. Whether the underlying exposure tracks anything residents actually experience
is a separate question, and it is the one we ask here.

Existing macroeconomic indicators are not well positioned to answer it. Equity market
performance, national unemployment, and aggregate wage growth are built to describe the
economy in total. They average over the local conditions that determine whether a paycheck
covers rent, and they report earnings in nominal terms, so a high wage expensive metro and
a low wage inexpensive county can appear far apart when the purchasing power behind those
wages is similar. The gap between what headline indicators measure and what families
experience locally is what motivates a county level analysis.

We ask how much the automatability of local jobs affects whether a county is affordable to
live in, and whether that relationship holds up once poverty and unemployment are
accounted for. To answer it we
build a county by year panel covering 2008 to 2023, excluding 2020, from eight datasets
published by four federal agencies. Each county year is summarized by four task groups, routine cognitive,
routine manual, non routine cognitive, and non routine manual, following the task
framework of @autor2003skill and the occupation taxonomy of @AutorDorn2013. The outcome is
an affordability salary, county median household income divided by the local price level.
We estimate a panel regression with year indicators and county clustered standard errors
to recover an interpretable effect size, use a RESET test to check whether a linear
specification is adequate, and then turn to random forest and neural network models to
capture the structure the linear model leaves behind. Every result we report is
associational.
